stimuli.title: Experiment
stimuli.text:
Students cut identical cylinders of potato tissue, recorded the mass of each, and placed three cylinders in each of five sucrose solutions in open beakers at 22 degrees C. After 24 hours they blotted and reweighed the cylinders. The mean percent change in mass for each solution is shown below.

| Sucrose concentration (M) | Mean change in mass (%) |
|---|---|
| 0.0 | +18 |
| 0.2 | +7 |
| 0.4 | -4 |
| 0.6 | -12 |
| 0.8 | -17 |

stimuli.title: Experiment
stimuli.text:
Students tested how temperature affects catalase, an enzyme that breaks hydrogen peroxide down into water and oxygen gas. In each trial they mixed the same volume of yeast extract with the same volume of 3% hydrogen peroxide at one temperature and collected the oxygen released in the first minute. Each temperature was tested three times; the means are shown below.

| Temperature (degrees C) | Oxygen released (mL per minute) |
|---|---|
| 10 | 4.0 |
| 20 | 7.5 |
| 30 | 11.0 |
| 40 | 12.5 |
| 50 | 6.0 |
| 60 | 0.5 |

stimuli.title: Experiment
stimuli.text:
In a model cell, hormone H binds a receptor in the plasma membrane. The receptor activates protein A, protein A activates kinase B, and kinase B phosphorylates transcription factor C, which then turns on gene G. Researchers studied four cell lines, each with the change shown, and recorded whether gene G was expressed.

| Cell line | Change | Gene G expressed? |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | None | Only when H is added |
| 2 | Receptor cannot bind H | Never |
| 3 | Kinase B is always active | Always, with or without H |
| 4 | Factor C cannot be phosphorylated | Never |

stimuli.title: Experiment
stimuli.text:
In a species of plant, purple flowers (P) are dominant to white flowers (p), and tall stems (T) are dominant to short stems (t). A researcher crossed two plants that were heterozygous for both genes (PpTt x PpTt) and classified 320 offspring.

| Phenotype | Observed number |
|---|---|
| Purple, tall | 190 |
| Purple, short | 50 |
| White, tall | 62 |
| White, short | 18 |

Chi-square critical values at p = 0.05: 1 degree of freedom 3.84, 2 degrees 5.99, 3 degrees 7.81.

stimuli.title: Data
stimuli.text:
Researchers measured the amount of mRNA from three genes in liver cells and in skeletal muscle cells taken from the same mouse. Amounts are in relative units.

| Gene | Liver cells | Muscle cells |
|---|---|---|
| Albumin (a blood protein) | 95 | 1 |
| Myosin (a muscle motor protein) | 2 | 88 |
| Actin (a cytoskeleton protein) | 40 | 45 |

stimuli.title: Data
stimuli.text:
In a population of moths, wing color is controlled by one gene with two alleles: D (dark, dominant) and d (light, recessive). Researchers sampled 1,000 moths in 2020. Over the next five years, the bark of the trees where the moths rest became much lighter. They sampled 1,000 moths again in 2025.

| Genotype | Moths in 2020 | Moths in 2025 |
|---|---|---|
| DD | 360 | 250 |
| Dd | 480 | 450 |
| dd | 160 | 300 |

stimuli.title: Data
stimuli.text:
On an island, researchers measured the beak depth of a population of seed-eating finches before and after a drought. During the drought, most small, soft seeds disappeared, leaving mainly large, hard seeds.

| Group | Birds measured | Mean beak depth (mm) |
|---|---|---|
| Before the drought | 750 | 9.2 |
| Survivors after the drought | 180 | 9.8 |
| Offspring of survivors | 220 | 9.7 |

stimuli.title: Data
stimuli.text:
Forty rabbits were released into a large fenced grassland with no predators. Researchers counted the population each year.

| Year | Rabbits |
|---|---|
| 0 | 40 |
| 1 | 80 |
| 2 | 160 |
| 3 | 300 |
| 4 | 420 |
| 5 | 470 |
| 6 | 480 |
| 7 | 475 |

questions.stem: Water moves up the xylem of a tall tree as an unbroken column, pulled from above as water evaporates from the leaves. Which property of water most directly keeps the column from breaking?
questions.explanation: Hydrogen bonds between water molecules (cohesion) let a pull at the top of the column be passed all the way down. A high specific heat stabilizes temperature but does not hold the column together, and water's bonds are polar.

questions.stem: Bacteria are grown in a medium whose only nitrogen source contains the heavy isotope 15N. After several generations, which molecules in the cells will contain the most 15N?
questions.explanation: Nitrogen is part of every amino acid and every nitrogenous base, so proteins and nucleic acids take up the label. Carbohydrates and fatty acids are made of carbon, hydrogen and oxygen only.

questions.stem: When two glucose monomers are joined by a covalent bond to form a disaccharide, what else is produced?
questions.explanation: Joining monomers is dehydration synthesis: an -OH from one monomer and an -H from the other leave as one water molecule for each bond formed. Hydrolysis runs the other way, using water to break the bond.

questions.stem: A mutation replaces a nonpolar amino acid buried inside a globular enzyme with an amino acid that has a charged R group. The most likely effect is
options: no change to the primary structure
a change in folding and function
a broken peptide bond in the chain
questions.explanation: Nonpolar R groups cluster away from water in the protein's interior; a charged R group there disrupts the interactions that set tertiary structure, so the shape and function change. The substitution itself is a change in primary structure, not a broken bond.

questions.stem: Phospholipids placed in water form a bilayer on their own. They do this because each phospholipid has
options: two hydrophilic ends and no tails
a hydrophobic head and hydrophilic tails
a hydrophilic head and hydrophobic tails
questions.explanation: The polar phosphate head faces water and the nonpolar fatty acid tails face each other, which is the lowest-energy arrangement. A molecule that was nonpolar throughout would not orient into a sheet with two water-facing surfaces.

questions.stem: The two strands of a DNA double helix are described as antiparallel. This means that the strands
options: are linked to each other by covalent bonds
run in the same 5' to 3' direction
questions.explanation: One strand runs 5' to 3' and its partner runs 3' to 5', so the 5' end of one lies opposite the 3' end of the other. The strands are held together by hydrogen bonds between bases, and both use deoxyribose.

questions.stem: Viewed with an electron microscope, which structure would show that a cell is eukaryotic rather than prokaryotic?
questions.explanation: Only eukaryotic cells enclose their DNA in a nucleus bounded by a membrane envelope. Every cell, prokaryotic or eukaryotic, has ribosomes, a plasma membrane and cytoplasm.

questions.stem: A pancreatic cell makes a digestive enzyme that it secretes. After the enzyme is made on ribosomes, which path does it most likely follow?
questions.explanation: Secreted proteins are made by ribosomes on the rough ER, modified and sorted in the Golgi, and carried in vesicles that fuse with the plasma membrane. The Golgi comes after the ER, not before.

questions.stem: Cell A is a cube 1 micrometer on each side, and cell B is a cube 3 micrometers on each side. Which statement is correct?
options: Cell B exchanges more material per unit volume
The two cells have the same ratio
Cell B has the larger surface-to-volume ratio
Cell A has the larger surface-to-volume ratio
questions.explanation: Cell A: surface 6, volume 1, ratio 6. Cell B: surface 54, volume 27, ratio 2. Smaller cells have more membrane for each unit of volume, so they exchange materials more efficiently.

questions.stem: Which substance crosses a pure phospholipid bilayer most easily, with no help from a protein?
questions.explanation: Small nonpolar molecules such as O2 dissolve through the hydrophobic core of the bilayer. Ions, polar sugars and large molecules need channels, carriers or vesicles.

questions.stem: The sodium-potassium pump moves sodium ions out of a cell even though sodium is already more concentrated outside. This movement requires
questions.explanation: Moving a substance against its concentration gradient is active transport, and the pump uses the energy released by ATP hydrolysis. Channels and aquaporins only let substances move down their gradients.

questions.stem: A cell from an aquatic plant leaf is placed in a concentrated salt solution. Viewed under a microscope a few minutes later, the cell will most likely show
options: its cell wall dissolving in the salt
its membrane pulling away from the wall
its vacuole swelling until the cell bursts
questions.explanation: The salt solution is hypertonic, so water leaves the cell by osmosis; the central vacuole shrinks and the membrane pulls away from the rigid wall (plasmolysis). The wall keeps a plant cell from bursting even in pure water.

questions.stem: Which observation best supports the hypothesis that mitochondria descended from free-living prokaryotes?
options: They make ATP for the cell
They have their own circular DNA
They are found in plant cells
questions.explanation: Mitochondria carry circular DNA and ribosomes like those of bacteria and divide by a process like binary fission, which supports endosymbiosis. Making ATP or sitting in the cytoplasm says nothing about where they came from.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes the effect of temperature shown in the data?
options: The rate peaks near 40 degrees C, then falls
The rate falls steadily as temperature rises
The rate rises steadily across all temperatures
The rate is about the same at every temperature
questions.explanation: Oxygen production climbs from 4.0 to 12.5 mL per minute between 10 and 40 degrees C, then drops to 0.5 by 60 degrees C. The pattern is a peak, not a steady trend.

questions.stem: The best explanation for the very low rate at 60 degrees C is that
options: the enzyme's amino acid sequence changed
the molecules moved too slowly to collide
the enzyme denatured and lost its shape
the substrate was used up in the first seconds
questions.explanation: High temperature breaks the weak bonds that hold catalase's tertiary structure, so the active site no longer fits the substrate. Heat does not change the amino acid sequence, and molecules move faster, not slower, when warmer.

questions.stem: The best explanation for the increase in rate from 10 to 30 degrees C is
options: a larger amount of enzyme in each trial
a change in the shape of the active site
less hydrogen peroxide left to react
questions.explanation: Warmer molecules move faster, so the enzyme and substrate collide more often and the reaction speeds up until the enzyme begins to denature. The amount of enzyme was held constant in every trial.

questions.stem: By about what percent did the rate of oxygen release increase from 10 degrees C to 30 degrees C?
questions.explanation: Percent change = (11.0 - 4.0) / 4.0 x 100 = 175%. Dividing the change by the final value instead gives 64%, 4.0 / 11.0 gives 36%, and 7 is the change in mL per minute, not a percent.

questions.stem: Adding more substrate overcomes the effect of an enzyme inhibitor. The inhibitor most likely
options: competes with substrate for the active site
binds an allosteric site and changes its shape
questions.explanation: A competitive inhibitor occupies the active site; with enough substrate, substrate molecules win most of the binding and the rate recovers. A noncompetitive (allosteric) inhibitor lowers the rate however much substrate is added.

questions.stem: After an enzyme catalyzes a reaction, the enzyme molecule
options: is unchanged and can catalyze the reaction again
is used up and must be replaced
questions.explanation: An enzyme is a catalyst: it binds its substrate, speeds the reaction and is released unchanged, so one enzyme molecule can act many times.

questions.stem: Algae given water labeled with the heavy isotope oxygen-18 release labeled O2 gas. Algae given carbon dioxide labeled with oxygen-18 release unlabeled O2. These results show that the O2 released in photosynthesis
questions.explanation: Only the water label shows up in the O2, so the oxygen gas comes from water split in the light-dependent reactions. The oxygen atoms of carbon dioxide end up in sugar and in water made in the Calvin cycle.

questions.stem: A poison blocks the transfer of electrons to oxygen at the end of the electron transport chain in mitochondria. Which process stops making ATP almost at once?
questions.explanation: With electron flow stopped, protons are no longer pumped, the gradient across the inner membrane collapses and ATP synthase stops. Glycolysis and fermentation happen in the cytosol and do not depend on oxygen, and photophosphorylation runs on light in chloroplasts.

questions.stem: A neuron releases a neurotransmitter that diffuses across a narrow gap and binds receptors on a muscle cell. This is an example of
questions.explanation: The neurotransmitter acts on a nearby cell after crossing a small space, which is short-distance (local) signaling. Hormones travel long distances in the circulatory system.

questions.stem: Many signal transduction pathways amplify a signal. Amplification means that
options: one receptor binds many ligand molecules at once
one ligand leads to many activated molecules
the cell responds more slowly but longer
the ligand is copied by the target cell
questions.explanation: Each activated protein in a cascade can activate many copies of the next, so a single ligand binding produces a large response. The ligand itself is not copied.

questions.stem: Epinephrine binds a G protein-coupled receptor on a liver cell, and the level of cyclic AMP inside the cell rises. In this pathway, cyclic AMP acts as
questions.explanation: Epinephrine is the first messenger (ligand) and never enters the cell; cyclic AMP is a small molecule made inside that relays the signal. It activates protein kinases that carry the response forward.

questions.stem: A mutation makes a membrane receptor active even when no ligand is bound to it. The most likely result is
options: loss of the receptor from the membrane
a response that occurs all the time
no response even when ligand binds
questions.explanation: Everything downstream of the receptor is switched on continuously, so the cell responds whether or not the signal is present. Uncontrolled growth signals of this kind can contribute to cancer.

questions.stem: During childbirth, contractions of the uterus cause release of oxytocin, which causes stronger contractions and more oxytocin release. This is
questions.explanation: In positive feedback, the response increases the original stimulus, driving the process further until an endpoint, here delivery. Negative feedback would reduce the stimulus and return the body to a set point.

questions.stem: During which phase of the cell cycle is DNA replicated?
questions.explanation: DNA synthesis happens in the S (synthesis) phase of interphase. G1 and G2 are growth phases, and mitosis separates the already copied chromosomes.

questions.stem: A protein that halts the cell cycle when DNA is damaged is lost through mutation. Cells without the protein are more likely to
questions.explanation: Checkpoint proteins pause the cycle so damage can be repaired or the cell can undergo apoptosis. Without that brake, damaged cells keep dividing and mutations accumulate.

questions.stem: If the two genes assort independently, how many of the 320 offspring are expected to be purple and tall?
questions.explanation: Independent assortment predicts a 9:3:3:1 ratio, so 9/16 x 320 = 180 purple, tall plants. 190 is the observed number, and 240 (3/4) would be the expected number purple for one gene alone.

questions.stem: The chi-square value for these data, using the 9:3:3:1 ratio, is closest to
questions.explanation: Expected counts are 180, 60, 60 and 20. Chi-square = 10^2/180 + 10^2/60 + 2^2/60 + 2^2/20 = 0.56 + 1.67 + 0.07 + 0.20 = 2.5. 24 is the sum of the differences without squaring or dividing, and 7.8 is the critical value for 3 degrees of freedom.

questions.stem: Which conclusion is best supported by the chi-square test?
options: The two genes must be on one chromosome
questions.explanation: There are 4 classes, so 3 degrees of freedom and a critical value of 7.81. The calculated value of about 2.5 is smaller, so the differences can be due to chance and the hypothesis of independent assortment stands.

questions.stem: What is the probability that one offspring of this cross is white and short?
questions.explanation: White requires pp (1/4) and short requires tt (1/4). The genes assort independently, so multiply: 1/4 x 1/4 = 1/16.

questions.stem: Crossing over in prophase I increases genetic variation by
options: copying the DNA a second time
questions.explanation: Nonsister chromatids of homologous chromosomes swap segments, producing chromosomes with new combinations of alleles. Joining gametes is fertilization, another source of variation.

questions.stem: A woman who carries one copy of a recessive X-linked allele has children with a man who does not have the allele. What fraction of their sons are expected to show the trait?
questions.explanation: Sons get their only X from their mother, and she passes the allele on half the time. Their father gives sons a Y, so he has no effect on whether they show the trait.

questions.stem: DNA replication is semiconservative. After one round of replication, each new DNA molecule has
options: random pieces of old and new strands
one parental and one new strand
questions.explanation: Each parental strand serves as a template and stays paired with the new strand built on it. This was shown by density-labeling experiments with heavy nitrogen.

questions.stem: DNA polymerase can add nucleotides only to the 3' end of a growing strand. As a result, the lagging strand is made
options: in short fragments joined by ligase
from its 3' end toward its 5' end
questions.explanation: Because the lagging strand template runs the other way, polymerase must work away from the fork in short (Okazaki) fragments, which ligase joins. The leading strand is made continuously.

questions.stem: A segment of a template DNA strand reads 3'-TTGCAC-5'. What mRNA is transcribed from it?
questions.explanation: RNA polymerase builds mRNA complementary and antiparallel to the template, with U in place of T: 3'-TTG CAC-5' gives 5'-AAC GUG-3'. The option with T is DNA, and 5'-GUGCAA-3' is the right bases written in the wrong direction.

questions.stem: In eukaryotes, removing introns from pre-mRNA before it leaves the nucleus is called
questions.explanation: Splicing cuts out introns and joins the exons. Capping adds a modified guanine nucleotide to the 5' end, another processing step.

questions.stem: A tRNA has the anticodon 3'-GCA-5'. Which mRNA codon does it pair with?
questions.explanation: The anticodon pairs with the codon complementary and antiparallel: G with C, C with G, A with U, giving 5'-CGU-3'. CGT contains T, which is not found in mRNA.

questions.stem: In the lac operon of E. coli, when lactose is absent, the repressor protein
options: is broken down by the cell
binds lactose and lets go of the operator
questions.explanation: The active repressor binds the operator and keeps RNA polymerase from transcribing the genes. When lactose is present, a form of it binds the repressor, which then releases the DNA.

questions.stem: A single-base insertion near the start of a protein-coding gene usually has a large effect because it
options: has no effect on the protein
questions.explanation: Codons are read in groups of three from the start codon, so one extra base changes every codon after it and often brings an early stop codon. A substitution changes at most one codon.

questions.stem: In gel electrophoresis, DNA fragments move toward the positive electrode because DNA
questions.explanation: The phosphate groups of the backbone give DNA a negative charge, so it moves toward the positive pole. Shorter fragments move through the gel faster and travel farther.

questions.stem: Which condition must be present for natural selection to change a trait in a population?
questions.explanation: Selection acts on differences that are passed on: individuals with some heritable variants survive and reproduce more, so those variants increase. Equal survival means there is no selection.

questions.stem: During an antibiotic treatment, most bacteria in a patient die, but a few resistant ones survive and multiply. The best explanation is that
options: the bacteria learned to resist it
questions.explanation: Random mutations that give resistance were already in the population; the antibiotic removed the susceptible cells, so resistant ones made up the next generations. The environment selects variation; it does not create the needed mutations.

questions.stem: For many generations, dairy farmers chose the cows that produced the most milk to be the parents of the next generation. This is
questions.explanation: Humans, not the natural environment, chose which individuals reproduced, so the population changed toward higher milk yield. Drift is change by chance.

questions.stem: A storm kills 90% of a small beetle population at random, and the survivors carry allele frequencies different from those before the storm. This is
questions.explanation: A sudden, random reduction in population size is a bottleneck, a kind of genetic drift. The founder effect is drift when a few individuals start a new population elsewhere.

questions.stem: In a population in Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium, 16% of individuals show a recessive trait. What is the frequency of the dominant allele?
questions.explanation: The recessive phenotype is q^2 = 0.16, so q = 0.4 and p = 1 - 0.4 = 0.6. 0.4 is the recessive allele frequency, and 0.36 is p^2, the frequency of homozygous dominant individuals.

questions.stem: Which condition would help keep allele frequencies in a population from changing?
questions.explanation: Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium requires random mating, a large population, no migration, no mutation and no selection. Each of the other options is a cause of evolution.

questions.stem: The forelimbs of whales, bats and humans contain the same set of bones, arranged in different ways for different uses. These forelimbs are
questions.explanation: Homologous structures share an underlying plan inherited from a common ancestor even when their functions differ. Analogous structures look alike because of similar functions, not shared ancestry.

questions.stem: A cladogram shows frogs branching off first, then lizards, and then mice and humans as sister groups. Which pair shares the most recent common ancestor?
questions.explanation: Sister groups split from each other at the last node, so mice and humans share the most recent common ancestor. Frogs split off first and are the most distantly related of these to the others.

questions.stem: Two populations of birds live in the same forest, but they sing different songs and do not mate with each other. The barrier keeping them apart is
questions.explanation: Different courtship songs are a behavioral, prezygotic barrier. The birds share a forest, so it is not geographic; temporal isolation means breeding at different times.

questions.stem: Human babies of very low or very high birth weight have lower survival than babies of medium birth weight. This pattern is
questions.explanation: Selection against both extremes favors the middle and narrows the range, which is stabilizing selection. Disruptive selection would favor both extremes.

questions.stem: Which model best describes the growth of the rabbit population over the seven years?
questions.explanation: The population doubles at first, then slows and levels off near a maximum, the S-shaped curve of logistic growth. Exponential growth would keep accelerating.

questions.stem: The carrying capacity of the grassland for rabbits is closest to
questions.explanation: Carrying capacity (K) is the size at which the population levels off, here about 475 to 480. 240 is the size where logistic growth is fastest, about K/2, and 300 and 420 are counts from years when the population was still growing.

questions.stem: What was the average rate of population growth from year 0 to year 2?
questions.explanation: Rate = change in N / change in time = (160 - 40) / 2 years = 60 rabbits per year. 120 is the total change, not the change per year, 80 is the change from year 1 to year 2 alone, and 100 is the mean population size.

questions.stem: Which factor most likely slowed population growth after year 3?
options: A rise in the number of births
questions.explanation: As the population grows, each rabbit has less food, so birth rates fall and death rates rise: a density-dependent limit. There were no predators, and more births would speed growth.

questions.stem: The producers in a field store 20,000 kcal of energy. If about 10% passes to each higher level, about how much is available to secondary consumers?
questions.explanation: Primary consumers get about 10% of 20,000 = 2,000 kcal, and secondary consumers about 10% of that, 200 kcal. Most energy at each level is lost as heat from respiration.

questions.stem: When a predatory sea star was removed from a rocky shore, mussels took over the rocks and the number of species there dropped sharply. The sea star is best described as
questions.explanation: A keystone species has an effect on community structure far larger than its numbers; by eating mussels, the sea star kept space open for many other species.

questions.stem: A houseplant on a windowsill bends its stems toward the window. This growth response to light is
questions.explanation: A tropism is growth toward or away from a stimulus; photo- means light. Photoperiodism is a response to day length, such as the timing of flowering.

questions.stem: Which process returns carbon from living organisms to the atmosphere?
questions.explanation: Respiration by producers, consumers and decomposers releases CO2. Photosynthesis removes CO2 from the air, and transpiration releases water.

questions.stem: Cities on the coast often have milder summers and winters than inland cities at the same latitude. Which property of water best explains this?
questions.explanation: Water absorbs or releases a lot of heat for a small change in its own temperature, because heat first goes into breaking or forming hydrogen bonds. Large bodies of water therefore buffer the temperature of the air nearby.

questions.stem: In a water molecule, the oxygen atom carries a partial negative charge because
questions.explanation: Oxygen pulls the shared electrons of each O-H bond closer to itself, so it is partly negative and the hydrogens partly positive. Water is bent, not linear, which is why the charges do not cancel.

questions.stem: A plant takes up phosphate from the soil. Which molecules will the plant use the phosphorus to build?
questions.explanation: Phosphorus is part of the sugar-phosphate backbone of DNA and RNA and the head group of phospholipids (and ATP). Starch, cellulose, glucose and fatty acids contain no phosphorus.

questions.stem: Digestive enzymes break a protein down into its amino acids. This happens by
questions.explanation: Hydrolysis adds a water molecule across each bond to split polymers into monomers. Dehydration synthesis is the building reaction, and it releases water.

questions.stem: An enzyme heated to 90 degrees C loses its activity even though none of its peptide bonds are broken. Which level of structure has most likely been lost?
questions.explanation: Heat breaks the weak interactions (hydrogen bonds, hydrophobic interactions) that hold the folded three-dimensional shape. The amino acid sequence, its primary structure, is held by peptide bonds and is unchanged.

questions.stem: In a sample of double-stranded DNA from a bacterium, 18% of the bases are cytosine. What percent of the bases are thymine?
questions.explanation: Cytosine pairs with guanine, so G is also 18% and G + C = 36%. That leaves 64% for A + T, and since A pairs with T, thymine is 32%. Base pairing does not make A + T equal to 50%.

questions.stem: In which solutions was the potato tissue hypotonic to the sucrose solution?
questions.explanation: The tissue lost mass, so water left it, in 0.4, 0.6 and 0.8 M. Water moves from the hypotonic side to the hypertonic side, so in those beakers the solution was hypertonic and the tissue hypotonic.

questions.stem: Based on the data, the sucrose concentration with the same water potential as the potato cells is closest to
questions.explanation: Mass change crosses zero between 0.2 M (+7%) and 0.4 M (-4%). Interpolating, 7/11 of the way across gives about 0.33 M, so about 0.3 M is where there is no net water movement. At 0.4 M the tissue already lost mass.

questions.stem: Using solute potential = -iCRT, with i = 1 for sucrose, R = 0.0831 liter bars per mole per kelvin and T = 295 K, the water potential of the 0.2 M solution in its open beaker is closest to
questions.explanation: -(1)(0.2)(0.0831)(295) = -4.9 bars. In an open beaker the pressure potential is zero, so the water potential equals the solute potential.

questions.stem: Which change to the procedure would most improve confidence in the results?
options: Using one larger cylinder per solution
Weighing the cylinders only at the end
Testing more cylinders in each solution
questions.explanation: More replicates per solution reduce the effect of variation between cylinders and allow error bars. The 0.0 M solution is a useful control, and starting masses are needed to calculate percent change.

questions.stem: A cell lacks one functional digestive enzyme in its lysosomes. The cell will most likely
options: stop making proteins on its ribosomes
lose the lipids of its plasma membrane
be unable to make ATP by respiration
questions.explanation: Lysosomes hold hydrolytic enzymes that break down macromolecules and worn-out parts; without one enzyme, its substrate collects inside the lysosomes. ATP synthesis and protein synthesis happen elsewhere.

questions.stem: Aquaporins greatly speed the movement of water across some membranes. Water moving through aquaporins is
questions.explanation: Aquaporins are channel proteins: they provide a path but no energy, so water still moves only from higher to lower water potential. That is facilitated diffusion, a passive process.

questions.stem: Cholesterol is found among the phospholipids of animal cell membranes. Its main role there is to
options: pump ions out of the cell
questions.explanation: Cholesterol keeps the membrane from becoming too fluid when warm or too rigid when cold. Animal cells have no cell wall, and pumping ions is done by transport proteins.

questions.stem: Cells drive many energy-requiring (endergonic) reactions by
options: lowering the energy of the products
questions.explanation: Energy released when ATP is hydrolyzed is used to power the unfavorable reaction, often by phosphorylating a reactant. More enzyme speeds a reaction but cannot make an endergonic reaction proceed on its own.

questions.stem: The stomach enzyme pepsin works best near pH 2, and the intestinal enzyme trypsin works best near pH 8. The best explanation is that
options: each keeps its shape at its own pH
trypsin is denatured by basic conditions
both work best in neutral water
questions.explanation: The charges on R groups depend on pH, and they hold each enzyme's shape. Each enzyme has the most active shape at the pH of the place where it works.

questions.stem: The Calvin cycle uses which products of the light-dependent reactions?
questions.explanation: ATP and NADPH from the thylakoids supply the energy and electrons used to reduce carbon dioxide to sugar in the stroma. NADH and FADH2 are carriers in cellular respiration.

questions.stem: In a chloroplast, ATP synthase makes ATP as protons flow from
options: the matrix to the intermembrane space
the thylakoid space to the stroma
the stroma to the thylakoid space
questions.explanation: The light reactions pump protons into the thylakoid space, and they flow back out to the stroma through ATP synthase. The matrix and intermembrane space are parts of a mitochondrion.

questions.stem: In eukaryotic cells, the Krebs cycle takes place in the
questions.explanation: Pyruvate enters the mitochondrion and is oxidized in the matrix. Glycolysis happens in the cytosol.

questions.stem: Yeast moved from air into an oxygen-free flask keep making ATP by fermentation. The main role of fermentation is to
questions.explanation: Glycolysis needs NAD+ to accept electrons. Without oxygen, fermentation passes those electrons to pyruvate (or a product of it), regenerating NAD+ so glycolysis can keep making its 2 ATP per glucose.

questions.stem: A drug makes the inner mitochondrial membrane leaky to protons. Compared with untreated cells, treated cells would most likely
options: use less oxygen and make more ATP
make more ATP from each glucose
use more oxygen but make less ATP
questions.explanation: Electrons still flow to oxygen, and the chain speeds up as it keeps pumping protons that leak back; but the protons bypass ATP synthase, so less ATP is made and more energy is lost as heat.

questions.stem: The pigments in a leaf absorb mostly blue and red light. Under equal intensities, the rate of photosynthesis would be lowest in
questions.explanation: Green light is mostly reflected or transmitted, which is why leaves look green, so little of its energy drives the light reactions. White light contains the blue and red wavelengths.

questions.stem: After a meal, blood glucose rises, the pancreas releases insulin, and body cells take up glucose until blood glucose falls back to normal. This is
questions.explanation: The response (glucose uptake) reduces the stimulus (high blood glucose), returning the body to its set point. Positive feedback would push glucose further from normal.

questions.stem: Testosterone is a nonpolar steroid hormone that crosses the plasma membrane. Its receptor is most likely located
questions.explanation: A nonpolar hormone diffuses through the bilayer and binds an intracellular receptor, often one that acts as a transcription factor. Polar signals that cannot cross the membrane use surface receptors.

questions.stem: In many signaling pathways, protein kinases pass the signal along by
questions.explanation: A kinase transfers a phosphate from ATP to a target protein, switching it on (or off); a phosphorylation cascade relays the signal. Phosphatases remove phosphates and help turn the pathway off.

questions.stem: During which stage of mitosis do sister chromatids separate and move to opposite poles of the cell?
questions.explanation: In anaphase the proteins holding sister chromatids together break down and spindle fibers pull the chromatids to opposite poles. Chromosomes line up in metaphase and new nuclei form in telophase.

questions.stem: In a sample of onion root tip, 900 cells are in interphase and 100 are in mitosis. If one full cell cycle takes 20 hours, mitosis lasts about
questions.explanation: The fraction of cells in a phase estimates the fraction of time spent there: 100 / 1,000 = 0.1, and 0.1 x 20 hours = 2 hours. 18 hours is the time spent in interphase, and 10 hours would mean half the cells were in mitosis.

questions.stem: Mature nerve cells in adults usually no longer divide. They are most likely in
questions.explanation: Cells that stop dividing leave the cycle from G1 and enter G0, a nondividing state in which they still carry out their functions. Cells in S, G2 or metaphase are on their way to dividing.

questions.stem: During development, the cells between the fingers of a human embryo die in a controlled way, separating the fingers. This is
questions.explanation: Apoptosis is programmed cell death, an orderly self-destruction used to shape tissues. Necrosis is uncontrolled death from injury.

questions.stem: Independent assortment of chromosomes happens because
options: crossing over occurs in every meiotic cell
DNA is copied before meiosis begins
homologs orient randomly at metaphase I
sister chromatids split at anaphase II
questions.explanation: Each pair of homologs orients toward the poles independently of the other pairs, so a gamete gets a random mix of maternal and paternal chromosomes. Copying DNA does not create new combinations.

questions.stem: Red-flowered snapdragons crossed with white-flowered snapdragons give all pink offspring. A cross of two pink plants is expected to give
questions.explanation: Pink is the heterozygote under incomplete dominance. Crossing two heterozygotes gives 1/4 homozygous red, 1/2 pink and 1/4 homozygous white.

questions.stem: Two genes on the same chromosome are 12 map units apart. In a test cross of a heterozygote, what percent of offspring are expected to be recombinant?
questions.explanation: One map unit is defined as 1% recombination, so 12 map units means 12% recombinant offspring. The other 88% have the parental combinations; 50% recombinants is what unlinked genes give.

questions.stem: Hydrangea plants with identical genotypes make blue flowers in acidic soil and pink flowers in alkaline soil. This shows that
questions.explanation: The genotype is the same, so the difference in flower color comes from the soil. The environment changes how genes are expressed, not the genes themselves.

questions.stem: A disorder is caused by a mutation in mitochondrial DNA. It is usually passed on
options: from a mother to all her children
from a father to each of his sons
questions.explanation: Mitochondria in the zygote come from the egg, so mitochondrial genes follow the maternal line. They do not follow Mendel's ratios.

questions.stem: Nondisjunction during meiosis I produces gametes that
options: carry an extra or missing chromosome
have exactly half the usual chromosome number
questions.explanation: When homologs fail to separate, one daughter cell gets both and the other gets neither, so the gametes have n+1 or n-1 chromosomes. A normal gamete has exactly half the diploid number.

questions.stem: Which statement best explains the albumin data?
options: Albumin mRNA is made only after a mutation
The same genes are expressed differently
Liver cells contain more total DNA
Muscle cells lack the albumin gene
questions.explanation: Liver and muscle cells from one animal have the same genome; they differ in which genes are transcribed. Muscle cells keep the albumin gene but barely express it.

questions.stem: Actin mRNA is at similar levels in both cell types. The most likely reason is that actin
options: is needed by both types of cell
is made only in the nucleus
is not encoded in the DNA
questions.explanation: Genes for proteins every cell needs, such as cytoskeleton proteins, are expressed in most cell types. Genes for specialized jobs, such as albumin and myosin, are expressed in only some.

questions.stem: Which mechanism would most directly produce the difference in albumin mRNA between the two cell types?
options: Loss of DNA from the muscle cells
A different genetic code in each cell
questions.explanation: Transcription factors present in liver cells bind the albumin gene's regulatory sequences and recruit RNA polymerase. Every cell uses the same genetic code, and specialization does not remove genes.

questions.stem: A researcher hypothesizes that a liver protein, factor L, switches on the albumin gene. Which experiment best tests this?
options: Measure factor L in muscle cells only
Add factor L to muscle cells; measure albumin mRNA
Remove actin from liver cells; measure myosin mRNA
Count the albumin genes in each cell type
questions.explanation: If factor L is sufficient, making muscle cells produce it should raise their albumin mRNA, compared with muscle cells without it. Measuring factor L alone does not show cause.

questions.stem: During translation, peptide bonds form between amino acids at the
questions.explanation: The ribosome holds the mRNA and tRNAs and catalyzes peptide bonds between the amino acids they carry. In eukaryotes, transcription happens in the nucleus and translation in the cytoplasm.

questions.stem: Adding methyl groups to the DNA near a gene's promoter usually
questions.explanation: DNA methylation is an epigenetic change that tends to keep chromatin packed and genes silent. It changes expression without changing the sequence of bases.

questions.stem: A point mutation changes the codon GAA to GAG. Both codons code for glutamic acid. This mutation is
questions.explanation: A silent mutation changes a codon to another for the same amino acid, so the protein is unchanged; the genetic code is redundant. Missense changes the amino acid and nonsense creates a stop codon.

questions.stem: PCR is used to
options: insert a gene into a plasmid
make many copies of a DNA segment
questions.explanation: The polymerase chain reaction uses primers, heat-stable DNA polymerase and repeated heating and cooling to double a chosen segment each cycle. Restriction enzymes cut DNA and electrophoresis sorts it by size.

questions.stem: What was the frequency of the d allele in the moth population in 2020?
questions.explanation: Count d alleles: 2 x 160 (dd) + 480 (Dd) = 800 out of 2,000 alleles, so d = 0.4. 0.64 is the fraction of moths carrying at least one d (640 of 1,000), 0.48 is the fraction of heterozygotes, and 0.6 is the frequency of D.

questions.stem: Do the 2020 genotype counts fit Hardy-Weinberg proportions?
options: No, there are too many heterozygotes
No, there are too few dd moths
Yes, they match the expected counts
No, the D allele is too rare
questions.explanation: With p = 0.6 and q = 0.4, the expected frequencies are p^2 = 0.36, 2pq = 0.48 and q^2 = 0.16, or 360, 480 and 160 moths: exactly what was observed.

questions.stem: The frequency of the d allele in 2025 is closest to
questions.explanation: d alleles: 2 x 300 + 450 = 1,050 of 2,000, so d = 0.525, about 0.53. 0.30 is the fraction of dd moths, not the allele frequency.

questions.stem: Which explanation best fits the change between 2020 and 2025?
options: Dark moths turned into light moths
Moths chose bark that matched their color
Light moths survived better on the new bark
questions.explanation: On light bark, light moths were harder for predators to see, so more of them survived and passed on d. Individuals do not change genotype, and the population moved away from, not toward, its earlier equilibrium.

questions.stem: In evolutionary terms, the fittest individual in a population is the one that
questions.explanation: Fitness is reproductive success: the number of offspring that survive and reproduce. A long life or great strength matters only if it leads to more offspring.

questions.stem: Comparing the amino acid sequence of a protein that all eukaryotes share supports common ancestry because
options: the sequence stays the same over long periods of time
the protein is found only in animals
every species has the same sequence
questions.explanation: Shared sequences point to a common origin, and the number of differences grows with time since two lineages split. If the sequence never changed, it could not reveal relationships.

questions.stem: A few birds blown to a distant island start a new population whose allele frequencies differ from those on the mainland. This is
questions.explanation: A small group starting a new population carries only a sample of the original alleles, by chance. A bottleneck is a sharp drop in an existing population's size.

questions.stem: Wind carries pollen back and forth between two populations of the same plant species. Over time, this gene flow tends to
options: cause a new species to form
lower the variation in each one
questions.explanation: Moving alleles between populations evens out their allele frequencies and works against divergence. It adds alleles to each population, increasing their variation.

questions.stem: Sharks and dolphins have similar streamlined bodies and fins, but sharks are fish and dolphins are mammals. Their similar body shapes are best explained by
questions.explanation: Similar environments selected for similar shapes in unrelated lineages, producing analogous traits. Their common ancestor lived long ago and did not have this body form.

questions.stem: Experiments that pass electric sparks through mixtures of simple gases like those of early Earth produce amino acids. These results support the idea that
options: amino acids came only from meteorites
the first cells used DNA as their genome
organic molecules can form without life
early air was rich in free oxygen
questions.explanation: The experiments showed that small organic molecules can form from inorganic ones under early-Earth conditions. They say nothing about DNA, and the gas mixtures used had no free oxygen.

questions.stem: Small cleaner fish eat parasites off the skin of larger fish. The cleaners get food and the larger fish lose their parasites. This relationship is
questions.explanation: Both species benefit, which is mutualism. In commensalism one benefits and the other is unaffected.

questions.stem: Compared with a lizard of the same body mass, a mouse must eat much more food each day. The main reason is that the mouse
questions.explanation: Endotherms use energy from food to generate body heat, so their metabolic rate is far higher than that of an ectotherm of the same size, which relies on outside heat.

questions.stem: Which factor limits a population regardless of how dense the population is?
questions.explanation: A hurricane kills a similar fraction of a population whether it is crowded or sparse, so it is density-independent. Disease, competition and predation all intensify as density rises.

questions.stem: Bacteria in soil and in root nodules convert nitrogen gas from the air into ammonia that plants can use. This process is
questions.explanation: Nitrogen fixation turns N2, which plants cannot use, into ammonia. Denitrification does the reverse, returning nitrogen gas to the air.

questions.stem: A plant introduced to a new region spreads rapidly and crowds out native plants. The most likely explanation is that it
questions.explanation: Invasive species often escape the herbivores, diseases and competitors that limited them at home, so their populations grow unchecked. Low genetic variation would be a disadvantage.

questions.stem: An ecosystem with high biodiversity is usually more resilient to disturbance because
options: other species can fill lost roles
questions.explanation: With many species, if one declines another with a similar role can take its place, so the ecosystem's processes keep running. Low diversity leaves no backup.

questions.stem: A pond sample has 10 fish: 5 of species A, 3 of species B and 2 of species C. Using Simpson's diversity index, 1 minus the sum of (n/N)^2, the index is
In the food chain grass, grasshopper, frog, snake, the frog is a
questions.explanation: Grass is the producer, the grasshopper eats it (primary consumer), and the frog eats the grasshopper (secondary consumer). The snake is the tertiary consumer.

questions.stem: Ice floats on liquid water. The best explanation is that in ice, water molecules
options: trap bubbles of air between them
are held in an open lattice by hydrogen bonds
are packed together more tightly than in liquid water
lose their polarity as they freeze
questions.explanation: As water freezes, each molecule hydrogen bonds to four neighbors in a spaced-out lattice, so ice is less dense than liquid water. The molecules remain polar; that polarity is what forms the lattice.

questions.stem: Water rises up a narrow glass tube above the level of the water around it. The attraction of water molecules to the glass is called
questions.explanation: Adhesion is attraction between water and a different substance, here the polar glass. Cohesion is the attraction of water molecules to each other, which then pulls more water up behind.

questions.stem: Which type of macromolecule is most likely to contain sulfur?
questions.explanation: Some amino acids, such as cysteine and methionine, contain sulfur, so proteins do. Carbohydrates, nucleic acids and triglycerides do not.

questions.stem: Compared with an unsaturated fatty acid, a saturated fatty acid
options: is usually liquid at room temperature
has one or more double bonds
questions.explanation: Saturated means every carbon holds as many hydrogens as it can, so there are no C=C double bonds; the straight chains pack tightly and the fat is solid at room temperature. Double bonds put kinks in unsaturated chains.

questions.stem: Which pairing of a monomer with the polymer it builds is correct?
questions.explanation: RNA is a polymer of nucleotides. Starch is a polymer of glucose and proteins are polymers of amino acids.

questions.stem: Proteins have directionality. During synthesis, each new amino acid is added to which end of the growing polypeptide?
options: The R group of the last amino acid
questions.explanation: A polypeptide grows from its amino terminus toward its carboxyl terminus: each new amino acid bonds to the carboxyl group at the end of the chain. The amino terminus is the first amino acid made.

questions.stem: Which components make up a single DNA nucleotide?
options: An amino group, a carboxyl group and a side chain
Glycerol, a phosphate and two fatty acids
A phosphate, a five-carbon sugar and a base
A phosphate, a six-carbon sugar and a base
questions.explanation: Each nucleotide has a phosphate group, the five-carbon sugar deoxyribose and a nitrogenous base. Glycerol with fatty acids describes a lipid, and an amino and carboxyl group describe an amino acid.

questions.stem: Which feature is found in RNA but not in DNA?
questions.explanation: RNA uses uracil in place of thymine and ribose in place of deoxyribose. Both nucleic acids have a sugar-phosphate backbone.

questions.stem: Alpha helices and beta pleated sheets in a protein are held in shape mainly by
questions.explanation: Secondary structure comes from hydrogen bonds between backbone atoms of the polypeptide. Interactions among R groups, including disulfide bonds, shape the tertiary structure.

questions.stem: Hemoglobin is made of four polypeptide chains held together. This arrangement of chains is the protein's
questions.explanation: Quaternary structure is the association of two or more polypeptide subunits. Tertiary structure is the folding of a single chain.

questions.stem: Which feature do chloroplasts and mitochondria share?
questions.explanation: Both organelles are bounded by two membranes, consistent with their origin by endosymbiosis. Chlorophyll and thylakoids are found only in chloroplasts.

questions.stem: Liver cells that break down many drugs and toxins would be expected to have a large amount of
questions.explanation: The smooth endoplasmic reticulum holds enzymes that detoxify drugs and also makes lipids. Nucleoli make ribosomal subunits and centrioles help organize the spindle.

questions.stem: The inner membrane of a mitochondrion is folded into many cristae. The most likely advantage of the folding is
questions.explanation: The electron transport chain and ATP synthase sit in the inner membrane, so folding packs more of them into the same space. More membrane surface means more ATP made.

questions.stem: A plant cell placed in pure water swells but does not burst because
options: its cell wall pushes back on it
it exports all of its solutes
questions.explanation: Water enters until the pressure of the stretched wall (pressure potential) balances the pull of the solutes; the cell becomes turgid. Water crosses the membrane freely, through aquaporins and the bilayer.

questions.stem: A membrane protein uses the flow of H+ ions down their gradient to move sucrose into a cell against the sucrose gradient. Sucrose uptake would stop soonest if
options: the cell made more of the protein
questions.explanation: This is cotransport: the energy comes from the H+ gradient, which proton pumps build using ATP. Without the gradient there is no energy to move sucrose uphill.

questions.stem: A white blood cell engulfs a bacterium by wrapping its plasma membrane around it. This process is
questions.explanation: Phagocytosis is endocytosis of large particles: the membrane surrounds the particle and pinches off as a vesicle. Exocytosis moves material out of the cell.

questions.stem: Neurons release neurotransmitter molecules stored in vesicles. The vesicles fuse with the plasma membrane and spill their contents outside. This is
questions.explanation: In exocytosis, a vesicle fuses with the plasma membrane and releases its contents outside the cell. Endocytosis and pinocytosis bring material in.

questions.stem: A freshwater protist lives in water that is hypotonic to its cytoplasm. Which structure helps it avoid bursting?
questions.explanation: Water keeps flowing into the protist by osmosis, and the contractile vacuole collects it and expels it. Lysosomes digest material and ribosomes make proteins.

questions.stem: One advantage of membrane-bound organelles in eukaryotic cells is that they
options: remove the need for any ribosomes
questions.explanation: Separate compartments keep different conditions, such as the acid inside lysosomes, so reactions that would interfere can run at the same time. Eukaryotic cells still need ribosomes and a plasma membrane.

questions.stem: A plant cell has a solute potential of -0.6 MPa and a pressure potential of 0.2 MPa. What is its water potential?
questions.explanation: Water potential is the sum of pressure potential and solute potential: 0.2 + (-0.6) = -0.4 MPa. Subtracting the pressure potential instead would give -0.8.

questions.stem: The final product of a metabolic pathway binds to an enzyme early in the pathway and slows it down. This is
questions.explanation: In feedback inhibition, a product shuts down its own production, often by binding an allosteric site on the first enzyme. The pathway slows when product is plentiful and speeds up when it is used.

questions.stem: A metal ion such as zinc that must bind to an enzyme for the enzyme to work is
questions.explanation: Cofactors are nonprotein helpers, such as metal ions, that an enzyme needs to function; organic cofactors are coenzymes. The substrate is the molecule the enzyme acts on.

questions.stem: Which process converts light energy into chemical energy stored in sugars?
questions.explanation: Photosynthesis captures light energy and stores it in the bonds of carbohydrates. Respiration, fermentation and glycolysis release energy stored in sugars.

questions.stem: Glycolysis takes place in the cytosol. Its products include
questions.explanation: Glycolysis splits glucose into two pyruvate, with a net gain of 2 ATP and 2 NADH. Carbon dioxide and FADH2 come from the Krebs cycle in the mitochondrion.

questions.stem: As substrate concentration rises, the rate of an enzyme-catalyzed reaction levels off. The best explanation is that
questions.explanation: At high substrate concentration nearly every enzyme molecule is busy, so adding substrate cannot raise the rate further. Only more enzyme would.

questions.stem: In the light-dependent reactions, the electrons lost by chlorophyll in photosystem II are replaced by electrons from
questions.explanation: Photosystem II splits water, taking its electrons and releasing O2 and H+. NADPH is where the electrons end up, at the end of the chain.

questions.stem: In aerobic respiration, the final electron acceptor of the electron transport chain is
questions.explanation: Oxygen accepts electrons at the end of the chain and combines with H+ to form water. Water is the product, not the acceptor.

questions.stem: A plant in a sealed chamber takes up 24 mL of carbon dioxide in 8 minutes. What is its average rate of carbon dioxide uptake?
questions.explanation: Rate = amount of change / change in time = 24 mL / 8 min = 3 mL per minute. Dividing time by volume gives 0.33, and multiplying gives 192.

questions.stem: Per molecule of glucose, aerobic respiration yields far more ATP than fermentation because
options: fermentation uses ATP instead of making it
glycolysis runs much faster when oxygen is present
oxygen is converted directly into ATP
pyruvate is fully oxidized in the mitochondria
questions.explanation: With oxygen, pyruvate is broken down to CO2 and the electrons feed the electron transport chain, which drives most ATP synthesis. Fermentation stops after glycolysis, so only 2 ATP are made per glucose.

questions.stem: A reaction that releases free energy is described as
questions.explanation: Exergonic reactions have a negative free energy change and release energy. Endergonic reactions absorb free energy, and building molecules (anabolism) is usually endergonic.

questions.stem: Which cell line serves as the control in this study?
questions.explanation: Line 1 has no change, so it shows what the normal pathway does; each mutant line is compared with it.

questions.stem: Line 3 cells are given a drug that stops the receptor from binding hormone H. Gene G in these cells would most likely
questions.explanation: Kinase B is downstream of the receptor and already active in line 3, so it keeps phosphorylating factor C whatever happens at the receptor. Blocking a step upstream of a stuck-on step has no effect.

questions.stem: A new cell line has a mutation that keeps protein A from activating kinase B. If hormone H is added, gene G would most likely
options: be turned on by protein A alone
questions.explanation: The signal cannot pass from protein A to kinase B, so factor C is never phosphorylated, just as in line 4. The result would match lines 2 and 4: no expression.

questions.stem: Some bacteria release a signal molecule and change their behavior only when its concentration is high. This quorum sensing lets a population
options: act together once it is dense
questions.explanation: The signal builds up as the population grows, so a response begins only when enough cells are present to make it effective, such as forming a biofilm. Bacteria divide by binary fission, not mitosis.

questions.stem: The signal molecule that binds specifically to a receptor protein is called the
questions.explanation: A ligand fits a receptor's binding site, and binding changes the receptor's shape, starting transduction. Second messengers are made inside the cell afterward.

questions.stem: Ripening fruit releases the gas ethylene, which causes nearby fruit to ripen and release still more ethylene. This is
questions.explanation: The response (more ethylene) strengthens the stimulus, so ripening spreads and speeds up. Negative feedback would damp the stimulus.

questions.stem: During which stage of mitosis do the chromosomes line up along the middle of the cell?
questions.explanation: At metaphase the spindle aligns the chromosomes at the cell's equator. In anaphase the sister chromatids separate and move to opposite poles.

questions.stem: Cyclin levels rise and fall during the cell cycle. Cyclins help control the cycle by
options: breaking down the nuclear envelope directly
questions.explanation: A cyclin binds and activates a cyclin-dependent kinase (Cdk), which phosphorylates proteins that move the cell past a checkpoint. When the cyclin is destroyed, the Cdk switches off.

questions.stem: Cancer cells often divide without the growth signals that normal cells need. This most directly reflects a loss of
questions.explanation: Mutations in genes that regulate checkpoints and growth signaling let cells pass through the cycle unchecked. The other features are not what limits normal division.

questions.stem: Compared with the same cell in G1, a cell in G2 has
questions.explanation: The cell copies its DNA in S phase, between G1 and G2, so a G2 cell has double the G1 amount. Mitosis then halves it again for each daughter cell.

questions.stem: A cell with 2n = 10 undergoes meiosis. How many chromatids does each cell have at the end of meiosis I?
questions.explanation: Meiosis I separates homologs, so each cell gets 5 chromosomes, but each is still made of two sister chromatids: 5 x 2 = 10. The chromatids separate in meiosis II, leaving 5 in each gamete.

questions.stem: An organism has 2n = 6. Counting independent assortment alone, how many genetically different gametes can it make?
questions.explanation: With n = 3 pairs, each assorting independently, there are 2^3 = 8 combinations. Crossing over would add many more.

questions.stem: To learn whether a purple-flowered plant is homozygous or heterozygous for a dominant purple allele, you should cross it with
questions.explanation: In a test cross with a homozygous recessive plant, any white offspring reveal a hidden recessive allele in the purple parent. All purple offspring suggest the parent is homozygous.

questions.stem: A heterozygous plant (Aa) is crossed with a homozygous recessive plant (aa). What fraction of the offspring are expected to show the recessive phenotype?
questions.explanation: Aa x aa gives Aa and aa in equal numbers, so half the offspring are aa and show the recessive trait. 1/4 is the answer for Aa x Aa.

questions.stem: A person with type AB blood makes both the A antigen and the B antigen on red blood cells. This is
questions.explanation: In codominance both alleles are fully expressed side by side. In incomplete dominance the heterozygote has an intermediate blend.

questions.stem: In a cross of AaBb x aabb, with the genes assorting independently, what is the probability of an aabb offspring?
questions.explanation: Aa x aa gives aa half the time, and Bb x bb gives bb half the time: 1/2 x 1/2 = 1/4. 1/16 would apply to AaBb x AaBb.

questions.stem: Two parents who do not show a trait have a daughter who does. The trait is most likely inherited as
questions.explanation: Unaffected parents with an affected child means the trait is recessive. An X-linked recessive daughter would need an affected father, so the trait must be autosomal recessive.

questions.stem: Human height varies continuously across a wide range. This pattern is typical of
options: a single gene with two alleles
questions.explanation: Many genes, each adding a little, plus environmental effects such as nutrition, give a smooth bell-shaped range of phenotypes. A single gene with two alleles gives a few distinct classes.

questions.stem: Homologous chromosomes separate from each other during
questions.explanation: Homologs separate in anaphase I, halving the chromosome number. Sister chromatids separate in anaphase II and in mitosis.

questions.stem: Recessive X-linked traits are more common in males than in females because males
options: get the allele on the Y
questions.explanation: A male has a single X, so one recessive allele is enough to show the trait; a female needs two copies. Males inherit their X from their mother.

questions.stem: Which enzyme unwinds the double helix at the replication fork?
questions.explanation: Helicase breaks the hydrogen bonds between base pairs and separates the strands. Ligase joins fragments, and DNA polymerase builds the new strands.

questions.stem: As the helix unwinds, the DNA ahead of the replication fork becomes overwound. Which enzyme relieves this strain?
questions.explanation: Topoisomerase cuts, rotates and rejoins DNA strands to release the twisting caused by unwinding. Helicase causes the unwinding in the first place.

questions.stem: A mutation changes a codon in the middle of a gene into a stop codon. The protein made will most likely be
questions.explanation: Translation ends at the new stop codon, so the polypeptide is cut short and is usually nonfunctional. This is a nonsense mutation.

questions.stem: One eukaryotic gene can code for several different proteins through
questions.explanation: Different combinations of exons can be joined from the same pre-mRNA, producing different mRNAs and proteins. Code redundancy means several codons give one amino acid, the reverse situation.

questions.stem: RNA polymerase binds to which region of DNA to start transcription?
questions.explanation: The promoter, upstream of the gene, is where RNA polymerase (with transcription factors in eukaryotes) attaches. The start codon is a sequence in mRNA read by the ribosome.

questions.stem: Bacteria can pick up a plasmid carrying an antibiotic resistance gene from other bacteria. This is
questions.explanation: Transformation, transduction and conjugation move genes between existing bacteria, adding genetic variation without reproduction. Binary fission copies the cell's own genes into two daughter cells.

questions.stem: A circular plasmid is cut by a restriction enzyme that has 3 sites in the plasmid. How many DNA fragments result?
questions.explanation: A circle cut in n places gives n pieces, so 3 cuts give 3 fragments. A straight piece of DNA cut 3 times would give 4.

questions.stem: Small regulatory RNA molecules that bind to a specific mRNA usually
questions.explanation: Small RNAs pair with complementary sequences on an mRNA and block its translation or mark it for breakdown, silencing the gene after transcription.

questions.stem: In prokaryotes, ribosomes can begin translating an mRNA before its transcription is finished because
questions.explanation: Prokaryotic DNA is in the cytoplasm, so ribosomes reach mRNA as soon as it is made. In eukaryotes the nuclear envelope separates transcription from translation.

questions.stem: After gel electrophoresis, which DNA fragment is found farthest from the wells?
questions.explanation: Small fragments slip through the pores of the gel more easily and travel farther in the same time. All DNA has about the same charge per unit length, so size, not base content, sets the distance.

questions.stem: The change in mean beak depth among the survivors is an example of
questions.explanation: The drought favored one extreme, deeper beaks that can crack hard seeds, so the mean shifted in one direction. Drift is random and would not track seed size.

questions.stem: Which observation best shows that beak depth is heritable?
options: Birds were measured in several groups
Offspring of survivors had deeper beaks
Fewer birds were alive after the drought
The seeds became larger and harder
questions.explanation: The survivors' offspring had a mean of 9.7 mm, close to their parents' 9.8 mm and above the earlier 9.2 mm, so the trait was passed on. Selection changes the next generation only for heritable traits.

questions.stem: The percent change in mean beak depth from before the drought to the survivors is closest to
questions.explanation: (9.8 - 9.2) / 9.2 x 100 = 6.5%. 24% is the fraction of birds that survived (180 of 750), and 76% is the fraction that did not (570 of 750).

questions.stem: Whales have small pelvic bones that do not support legs. These bones are
questions.explanation: Vestigial structures are reduced remnants of parts that had a function in ancestors, here four-legged land mammals. They are evidence of common ancestry.

questions.stem: In a population of seed-eating birds, those with very small or very large beaks survive better than those with medium beaks. This is
questions.explanation: Selection favors both extremes over the middle, which can split a population into two forms. Stabilizing selection favors the middle.

questions.stem: In a population in Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium, p = 0.7. What is the expected frequency of heterozygotes?
questions.explanation: q = 1 - 0.7 = 0.3, so 2pq = 2 x 0.7 x 0.3 = 0.42. 0.21 is pq without the 2, and 0.49 is p^2.

questions.stem: A horse and a donkey can mate and produce a mule, but mules cannot reproduce. This is an example of
questions.explanation: The barrier acts after a zygote forms: the hybrid is sterile. Prezygotic barriers, such as different songs or habitats, prevent mating or fertilization.

questions.stem: On a phylogenetic tree, a node where two branches split represents
questions.explanation: Each node stands for the common ancestor of the lineages that branch from it. Living species are at the tips of the branches.

questions.stem: The original source of new alleles in a population is
questions.explanation: Mutation creates new alleles; selection and drift only change the frequencies of alleles that already exist.

questions.stem: Populations with little genetic variation are at greater risk of extinction because
options: they have no mutations at all
fewer may resist a new disease
questions.explanation: With few variants, it is less likely that any individuals carry alleles that help them survive a new disease or change in environment. Genetic diversity gives selection something to act on.

questions.stem: Net primary productivity is the energy that
options: is lost as heat by consumers
questions.explanation: Gross primary productivity is all the energy producers capture; net is what remains after their own respiration, available for growth and for consumers.

questions.stem: A bacterial population of 500 cells grows exponentially with a maximum per capita growth rate of 0.2 per hour. Its population growth rate, dN/dt, is
questions.explanation: Exponential growth: dN/dt = rmax x N = 0.2 x 500 = 100 cells per hour. 600 is the population size after an hour of that growth, not the rate, and dividing 500 by 0.2 gives 2,500.

questions.stem: In logistic growth, a population grows fastest in number when N is
questions.explanation: dN/dt = rmax N (K - N)/K is largest at N = K/2, where there are many breeders and still plenty of resources. At K growth is zero.

questions.stem: Barnacles attach to a whale and are carried to new feeding areas, while the whale is neither helped nor harmed. This is
questions.explanation: One species benefits and the other is unaffected, which is commensalism. In parasitism the host is harmed.

questions.stem: Unlike the carbon cycle, the phosphorus cycle has no major
questions.explanation: Phosphorus moves from rocks to soil and water, through organisms and back to sediment, but has no significant atmospheric form. Carbon cycles through the air as CO2.

questions.stem: Fertilizer runoff causes an algal bloom in a lake, and weeks later many fish die. The fish die mainly because
options: the algae eat the fishes' food
the fertilizer itself is toxic to fish
questions.explanation: When the algae die, decomposers break them down and their respiration uses up the oxygen in the water. This is eutrophication.

questions.stem: Two species that need exactly the same limited resources cannot coexist forever in the same place; one will outcompete the other. This idea is
questions.explanation: The competitive exclusion principle says two species cannot share an identical niche. Resource partitioning, using resources differently, is how similar species manage to coexist.

questions.stem: A honeybee returning to the hive performs a dance that shows other bees the direction and distance of food. This behavior is an example of
questions.explanation: Animals exchange information through signals such as dances, calls and chemicals, which changes the behavior of others and can raise fitness. Tropisms are growth responses of plants.

questions.stem: Which human activity most directly increases the amount of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere?
questions.explanation: Burning coal, oil and gas releases carbon stored for millions of years as CO2. Planting forests removes CO2 from the air.

questions.stem: Food chains rarely have more than four or five levels. The main reason is that
options: most energy is lost as heat
predators are too large to be eaten
matter is destroyed at each level
questions.explanation: Only about 10% of the energy at one level reaches the next; the rest is used and lost as heat, so too little remains to support many more levels. Matter is recycled, not destroyed.
